anchor: Rung 5 means one thing on every axis. On a product axis it is what Claude Prep (Blueprint 720, the certification study platform on this site) does on that function, read from its code at commit ae34174 (2026-11-13). Claude Prep is the anchor at product level 5 by definition: a clause at or below rung 5 that it fails when read literally sits at rung 6, unless the clause is essential to the function, in which case the clause stays and the axis records Claude Prep's literal level in blueprint_level. Where Claude Prep is weak by design (first run, tutoring, verified hands-on tasks, access at every width), rung 5 is what a complete product needs. On a subject axis rung 5 is the lab's fiction made real at full fidelity (Luis, 2026-11-11). Each rung is a list of numbered clauses; a rung holds when every clause holds, and rungs are cumulative. Levels are computed by level_rule.
level_rule: A lab has three levels. Its scope level is the highest level whose thresholds (scope.thresholds: organs, links, steering links and reach) its graph meets, counting up from level 1. Its product level and its subject level are each computed as min(lower median of its axis rungs, weakest axis + 2), over the product axes it carries and over its subject axes, and neither is placed above its scope level, because a half is a state of the whole lab and the lab is only as broad as its graph. The lab level is the lowest of the three, because level 5 means all three: every product function Claude Prep has, translated into the lab; the lab's fiction made real; and a graph of working organs as broad and as densely joined, over every unit of its subject (Luis, 2026-11-11 and 2026-11-13). An axis grade is a rung, never a level, and is shown with the lab's graph beside it.
na_policy: A lab may mark at most 3 product axes not applicable, each with a reason the independent rater checks. A weak axis is graded, not excused.
world_rule: A world line substitutes only the clauses it names; every other clause of the axis rung still holds. A world line that names no clause substitutes nothing.

stages.6: Adaptive: selection, depth or rendering reads the visitor's own local record, and the page shows with numbers what changed since the last visit. No other visitor's data is used. A rater seeds two different records, loads each, and compares what the page chooses.
stages.7: Shared: any state, run or record opens identically for another visitor from a link or an exported file, and two shared states compare side by side with the differences computed. No account is needed. A rater opens the link and the file in a fresh profile and compares the numbers.
stages.8: Creative: visitors contribute items, scenes, rules or paths as a file or a pull request; the same gates run in CI, the review decision is recorded in the repository, and the accepted entry is listed with its author. A rater counts accepted entries with a gate run and a review record in git.
stages.9: Knowledge: a versioned release with schema, licence, CITATION.cff, method and a reproducible build command produces the dataset or benchmark. A rater runs the build command and diffs the output against the release.
stages.10: Reference: the lab's reference ledger lists outside references (URL, date, quoted context), each verifiable, from at least 5 independent sources. A daily-return share counts only once Luis approves an opt-in counter; until then the ledger alone decides. An EU backend now exists that could carry opt-in counts later, and no rung depends on it. A rater opens each URL in the ledger.

evolution.principle: A level is a state of the whole lab, read three ways: how far each axis has climbed, how the axes stand on each other, and how broad and how joined the lab's graph of organs is. Each rung of an axis stands on rungs of other axes that make it possible or give it something to act on, so an axis rises when the axes beneath it have risen, and a rung built without its supports is empty. Up to level 5 the subject half gives the product half a mechanism that computes keys and checks, a live view and a model for lessons to draw on, a result of the visitor's own for missions to judge, and engine values an explaining agent may cite; the product half gives the instrument tests, tokens, data, a shell and keyboard paths. Up to level 5 the visitor's record reaches the instrument only through the goals the visitor sets, by which its data can be pivoted; at level 6 the record changes what the instrument shows and says. A clause that names a capability another axis builds at a higher rung holds over the instances that exist and extends when that capability arrives, and a ticket for it depends on the ticket that builds that capability. A feature that no rung stands on, and that stands on nothing, raises no level, and from level 3 neither does an organ that no other reads and that reads none. Each portrait describes a lab whose axes all stand at that rung; the level rule lets the weakest axis sit two rungs lower, and the checkpoint is where a lab names which axis, which half or which part of its graph holds it there.
evolution.emergence: A level is reached when something appears in the lab that the level below made possible and did not contain. What appears follows from the lab's concept, can be traced back to its seed, and could not have been written as a requirement at the level below, because it is a consequence of that level existing: of people using it, of the records it keeps, of two organs meeting, of the subject answering back. The portraits below say what labs at one level have in common; a lab's own story names what emerged there in its own terms. A lab plans one level above where it stands, and every level above that is a conjecture, rewritten after each level ships from what appeared. Ten levels listed in advance are a feature list, and this atlas accepts none as a plan.
evolution.analogy_rule: Claude Prep reaches level 5 on the product half for a learner preparing dated certification exams from a published canon. Its graph has nine organs: a Today view, lessons, drills (with their help panel, tutored mocks, warm-ups and the spaced review of misses, which all run in one runner), a timed mock exam with its exam report, a spaced flashcard deck, a progress view with a readiness checklist and calibration, a plan with exam dates and a pace meter, hands-on labs, and a tracker of the official courses. Seven of them form one graph joined by fourteen links; the labs and the course tracker stand apart, because no other organ computes anything from their state. A lab in another domain reaches a similar level 5 by orthogonal development: each organ is rebuilt on the lab's own instrument, matched by the work it does, held to the same depth and joined to the others at least as densely. The exam blueprint becomes the lab's canon and declared units; a question becomes a state of the instrument whose answer the engine computes or a recorded label gives (where a photon goes, which phrase of a claim lacks support, which missed day costs a habit curve most); a lesson becomes a walk through the instrument where each worked example is a state the engine computes and the reader decides before it is revealed; drills become practice on the instrument, and tutor steps become help on it that never names the answer; the mock becomes the summative challenge, built to the challenge blueprint and run on the instrument; the evidence rule becomes the lab's written rule for which actions count as unaided; the progress view becomes the visitor's state per declared unit beside readiness, a checklist of stated thresholds over the lab's own skill; flashcards become the spaced return of what the visitor missed; the plan becomes the path to the visitor's own goal; hands-on labs become missions whose check the engine runs; the official course map becomes the outside curriculum the bindings name; and the return view reads the others, as Claude Prep's Today view reads lessons, due cards, misses and readiness. A function leaves the lab only with its axis, marked not applicable under the na policy; no single organ is excused on its own. The analogy breaks in five places, and each lab writes down where it breaks for it. Claude Prep stores its answer keys with its items, while a lab computes its keys from its model or reads them from labels recorded on states of its instrument, so its practice can be no truer than its model or its labels. Claude Prep's subject half is low (the atlas estimates about 1, unaudited) and the app makes no model call, so on the six subject axes level 5 is the lab's fiction made real and Claude Prep offers nothing to copy. Where Claude Prep is weak by design (first run, tutoring coverage, verified tasks, access at every width), rung 5 asks more than it has, and its labs and course tracker, which stand apart from its graph, mark where a lab should join more than the anchor does. A lab with no right answers maps practice and evidence onto the visitor's own predictions and data, and may mark up to 3 product axes not applicable, each with a reason the rater checks. A copied surface, such as a quiz set beside the instrument, fails the own-instrument rule at rung 1; an organ that no other reads and that reads none adds no scope above level 2.

1.name: The specimen
1.portrait: The lab is one organ, or several that do not read each other: working parts a visitor can use on their own, each for one purpose. Each function the lab has exists once, in its simplest honest form, on the lab's own instrument. One documented address opens the main view and says what can be done there. One capability of the fiction shows, at least as a picture, a preset or a canned animation; its values come from a table typed into the page, and presets change the view. One exercise checks one answer and keeps it with its time and mode, a count of what the visitor did is shown, and the state survives a reload.
1.shift: At level 0 the lab is a name and a promise. At level 1 something runs, each function as one fixed instance on the lab's own instrument, and the rule is fixed that a quiz, a text or a picture set beside the instrument does not count, so every later rung is built on the instrument itself.
1.checkpoint: Which part holds the lab at level 1, its product half, its subject half or its graph; does every function that exists run on the lab's own instrument; and on the way to level 5, which second organ comes first, what will it read from the first, and which of Claude Prep's nine organs does it stand for?

2.name: The first loop
2.portrait: The lab computes, and its organs begin to read each other. One path runs end to end from the visitor's own free input, through a mechanism whose formulas sit in the source, to a live view, and one entry of the fiction runs that way; the entry view is alive at rest. A practice session gives feedback that names the right answer, the visitor's choice and the reason, and a record view turns the finished sessions into a state per declared unit, the first organ that computes from what another wrote. A lessons track cuts the subject into its declared units with a page each, a catalogue of missions keeps its step checklists per step, and one model call per action goes through the site route with a fallback good on its own. A lab whose axes all stand here has about five organs (the instrument, practice, the record view, lessons and missions); the scope floor is three organs and one link over a quarter of the declared units. The material is versioned data apart from the code, the record has a typed contract, and every claim on the page is tagged real or illustrative. Everything off the one path is still fixed.
2.shift: A level 1 lab shows values and accepts one answer. A level 2 lab computes values from what the visitor types and keeps the result, and for the first time one organ computes from another's output, so the visitor's work starts to travel inside the lab.
2.checkpoint: Does one entry of the fiction run end to end from typed input, with its formulas in the source and every claim tagged; which of product, subject and scope holds the lab here, and which declared units does no organ work on; and why is this not level 5: which entries still run on presets, and which of Claude Prep's nine organs has no counterpart on the lab's own instrument yet?

3.name: The accountable system
3.portrait: Each shared decision of the lab is made in one place: how an item renders, how a lesson is built, what counts as evidence, how the page looks and how values are computed; and its organs form one connected graph. A published model, named with its author and year, runs for every input the page accepts, every value carries its unit, and half of the fiction's inventory runs from the visitor's input. Every declared unit has a lesson in one schema, stepwise help stands on at least two items in five, and missions open their material inside the lab with a completion that can be reopened. An entry view computes the main next actions from the record, and its deep links land inside them. A lab whose axes all stand here has about six organs (the instrument, lessons, drills, missions, a record view with a state per unit, and the entry view); the scope floor is five organs joined in one graph by at least four links, the instrument among them, with half the declared units each worked on by two organs. A rater can trace any number, mark or verdict to a rule or a source.
3.shift: At level 2 one path works and the first organs touch. At level 3 the lab replaces its local decisions with one engine, one schema, one evidence rule and one model, and its organs form one connected graph, so a change made once holds everywhere and any claim can be traced to where it was decided.
3.checkpoint: Can a rater pick any number, mark or verdict and trace it to one stated rule or a cited source; which of product, subject and scope holds the lab here, and which declared units do fewer than two organs work on; and why is this not level 5: which organs hang on a single thread, which result never comes back to the visitor through another organ, and which of Claude Prep's nine organs has no counterpart on the lab's own instrument yet?

4.name: The interlocked lab
4.portrait: The organs choose what they do from what the others recorded, and the graph closes loops. Drills deal what the visitor has not seen, then what they last got wrong; lessons draw their checks from the visitor's misses and their rules feed the warm-ups; a spaced deck brings cards back by their grades; the revision sheet is built from the misses; and the tour reads the current numbers. A progress view holds a mastery grid and charts over time, the outside curriculum is mapped onto the units with done counts, and at least half the missions ship an offline check. The visitor drags or edits the subject itself and the model recomputes, most of the fiction runs in one continuous central scene, at least five outputs match published reference values within stated tolerances, the record exports as one file, and a newcomer reaches a first meaningful action through a guided flow in under two minutes. A lab whose axes all stand here has about eight organs; the scope floor is six joined organs and seven links, at least three of which steer, with a directed loop made of steering links, another organ reading what the visitor did on the instrument and three organs working on each of four fifths of the declared units.
4.shift: A level 3 lab applies one rule everywhere, and its organs show each other's results: a record view computes a state per unit from what practice recorded. A level 4 lab lets each organ choose what it does from what the others recorded: drills deal from the misses, lesson checks are drawn from them, the revision sheet is built from them and the deck schedules from the grades, so the visitor's work changes what the lab offers next. It is also checked against values published outside it.
4.checkpoint: Does a result made in one organ change what another offers the visitor next, and do at least five outputs match published values within stated tolerances; which of product, subject and scope holds the lab here, and which declared units does no organ practise and record; and why is this not level 5: which capability of the fiction runs below its depicted detail, and which of Claude Prep's nine organs has no counterpart on the lab's own instrument yet?

5.name: The fiction made real
5.portrait: The fiction is made real and the product around it is complete. Every entry of the fiction inventory runs from the visitor's own input at the detail its source depicts, inside the central scene, and a skeptic reading the sources finds no depicted capability missing. Every quantity in the scene comes from a published model, the page reports how many reference values fall within tolerance and explains each miss, and the intelligence plays the fiction's role with its gain over the engine measured. Every function Claude Prep has stands as an organ on the lab's own instrument, or its axis is marked not applicable under the na policy: a return view, lessons, practice with help on every exercise, a summative challenge, spaced return, a record view, a plan toward a goal date, missions the engine checks and a map of the outside curriculum. With the instrument that makes about ten organs; at least seven of them read each other in one graph through at least eleven links, five of which steer, two organs read what the visitor did on the instrument, and three organs work on every declared unit. The record carries one person across visits and devices.
5.shift: A level 4 lab is checked on samples and lives in one browser, which it leaves only as an exported file: five reference values, most of the fiction, half of its tasks with a check. A level 5 lab makes closed claims and shows the proof on its own page: an independent reading of the sources finds no depicted capability missing, a task completes only on a pass, and every score of readiness, accuracy or gain stands beside its stated threshold and its misses. The record follows the person to every device they use.
5.checkpoint: Given the sources and not the inventory, would a skeptic find a depicted capability missing; set beside Claude Prep organ by organ, which function has no counterpart on the lab's own instrument, and which organ still stands apart from the graph; and does the page show its own misses beside every score?

6.name: The lab that remembers
6.portrait: The lab reads one visitor's own local record through a model fitted to that visitor and becomes a different lab for them. Today's session is ordered from their due items and misses and sized to their daily budget; lessons, help and missions are chosen and sized from their evidence; the model of the subject reports its own error for their inputs and refuses inputs outside its validity; and the page says in numbers what changed since their last visit. An ability estimate with its interval and a forgetting curve per item are fitted to the visitor's answers, every organ chooses and sizes its work from them, and a forecast organ answers when an item will fade or where the visitor will stand on a date, with an interval. The organs that stood apart at level 5 now read the record, so the graph holds at least nine joined organs and sixteen links. No other visitor's data is used, and the parts of rungs 2 to 5 met only in part are complete.
6.shift: Up to level 5 the lab reads the visitor's record through fixed rules: unseen items first, then the last missed, cards on a fixed schedule. At level 6 it fits a model to that one visitor, an ability with its interval and a forgetting curve per item, every organ chooses and sizes its work from that model, and the page states in numbers what the record changed since the last visit.
6.checkpoint: Seed two records with the same latest answers and different histories, one right months ago and one right yesterday: does the lab choose different items, depth and next actions for each from its model of that visitor, show each estimate with its interval, and state in numbers what changed since that visitor's last visit?

7.name: The shared object
7.portrait: Every state the lab can reach is an object that can leave it. A link or an exported file reopens any run, view, record, readiness report, explained state or artefact of the fiction identically in a fresh browser with no account; a model run reproduces on another machine; a model output travels with its provenance; and two visitors act on one state in turns, with a visible history of who did what. A comparison organ opens two records of the whole lab, the visitor's own and a shared one, and computes their differences unit by unit; it reads the record view and the summative challenge, and the record view shows where the visitor stands against the shared record, for at least ten joined organs and nineteen links.
7.shift: A level 6 lab is private to one browser. A level 7 lab makes each of its states portable and reproducible, so a second person can open exactly what the first saw, check the numbers on their own machine and see how two results differ.
7.checkpoint: Opened from a link or an exported file in a fresh profile on another machine, does every state reproduce the same numbers, and does the comparison of two shared states compute their differences?

8.name: The open workshop
8.portrait: People other than the builders extend the lab. Visitors contribute items, lessons, hints, missions, model components, scenes, tools, explanations and paths as files or pull requests; the gates that guard the lab's own material run on each contribution in continuous integration; the review decision is recorded in the repository; and each accepted entry is listed with its author. A workshop organ on the page lets a contributor draft an entry, run the lab's gates on it and try it in practice and in a lesson before submitting it as a file, so practice and lessons read the draft, for at least eleven joined organs and twenty-one links. At least one accepted contribution comes from someone outside the builders.
8.shift: At level 7 others can open and verify the lab's states. At level 8 they can add to the lab itself, and the gates that once guarded the builders' own work become a public contract that decides what a stranger's contribution may change.
8.checkpoint: Which entry was contributed by someone outside the builders, which gates did it pass in continuous integration, where in the repository is its review recorded, and could it be added without editing a core file?

9.name: The citable source
9.portrait: The lab produces knowledge that exists apart from its page. A versioned release with a schema, a licence, a citation file, a written method and one reproducible build command produces its dataset or benchmark: the item bank, the lesson corpus, the misconception catalogue, the model's tables with their reference checks, the gold set with its evaluation, the record format with its merge vectors, or the conformance fixtures. A release organ on the page lets the visitor open a released dataset, filter it and place their own result in it, reading their record, and the instrument opens any released case, for at least twelve joined organs and twenty-three links. A rater runs the build command and the output matches the release.
9.shift: At level 8 the lab accepts contributions. At level 9 it emits releases that others can rebuild, cite and reuse without opening the lab, so what the lab knows outlives its interface.
9.checkpoint: Run on a clean checkout, does the build command reproduce the released dataset or benchmark file for file, and does the release carry its schema, licence, citation file and method?

10.name: The reference
10.portrait: Outside people point to the lab as a way into its subject. Its reference ledger lists at least five independent outside sources (courses, articles, forums, papers, documentation), none owned or controlled by Luis or the builders, each verified at its URL with its quoted context, that cite its start paths, lessons, practice sets, model, assistant, imagery or explanation, or the lab itself as the way to see the fiction. A citation organ lets the visitor pick any state of the lab and get a citation pinned to its release and link, with the verified outside references to that part listed beside it; it reads the release organ and the comparison organ, for at least thirteen joined organs and twenty-five links over every declared unit.
10.shift: Up to level 9 every rung is decided inside the repository, the outside contribution of level 8 included, which enters through a review the builders record. At level 10 the evidence lies outside it: the lab's standing rests on what independent people already do with it, verifiable at each link.
10.checkpoint: Do at least five independent sources, each verified at its URL, cite this lab as a way to learn or see its subject, with none owned or controlled by Luis or the builders, and does each still hold at the next check?

roots.lessons.2: The bindings declare the units, modules and weights, and the track splits the subject into them; no other axis has to exist first.

scope.principle: The axes say whether what a lab has is right; scope says how much of it there is and how it holds together. A lab is counted as a graph: its organs (the working parts a visitor uses on their own), its links (one organ computing from what another wrote) and its reach (the share of the subject's units its organs work on, and how many organs work on each). One well-made instrument passes the low rungs of every subject axis, because those rungs ask whether what exists is correct; alone it stays at scope level 1. It rises when other organs stand beside it and read each other; from level 3 it must be joined to them, and from level 4 one of them must read what the visitor did on it. Breadth counts only when it is connected: from level 3 an organ outside the largest connected part counts for nothing.
scope.organ: An organ is a working part of the lab that a visitor can use on its own for one purpose, on the real path of the visitor the lab is built for, with the access that visitor has; where organs sit behind credentials, the count says whose path it is. It passes three tests: it does work of its own kind (computes an answer, teaches a unit, runs a practice, holds a mission, computes a record, keeps a plan); it keeps or computes state that no other organ holds (the visitor's input or work in it, or a result only it produces); and it is no other organ seen another way. Views that draw the same values are one organ, and so is a part that only shows a shared selection; a part that keeps its own state and gives its own kind of result stays an organ when it follows a shared selection. Six plots of one measurement, a canvas, a tab, a panel, a narration or a tour of the instrument belong to the organ they show, and help shown on an exercise belongs to the organ whose exercise it helps. A list, shelf, history or picker of the runs, items or sessions one organ produced belongs to that organ; a record view is an organ only when it computes, across records, a state no single record shows (a state per unit, a trend, a readiness verdict) and the visitor acts on it. A box that answers questions about another organ's current state, or sets it, is that organ's narration or control, whatever engine it runs; an organ's own input is about the subject. One runner started with another filter, scope, unit or track is the same organ, and copies per track or per unit add reach, never organs. Calling the lab's engine does not merge parts: a practice session, a summative challenge, a mission check and a lesson's worked example that all compute their keys with the instrument's engine are separate organs when each keeps its own state (a session, a deadline and its flags, a mission's steps, a reader's place) and gives its own kind of result (a score, a verdict on readiness, a pass, a taught unit). The instrument is the organ that runs the lab's mechanism on the visitor's own input. The shell, navigation, search, settings, sync, editions and tests carry organs and are not organs.
scope.link: A link is one organ reading what another organ wrote, in a way the visitor can see: a result, a record or a choice the visitor made in the first organ changes what the second organ computes, orders, selects or offers as its next action, whether the second reads it directly or through a store or a digest. Each ordered pair of two different organs counts once, however many values or pages carry it. A link steers when what the first organ wrote changes what the second deals, orders or proposes next (an item, a card, a check, a mission, a next action); any other link shows. A panel that shows one organ's state on another organ's page belongs to the organ it shows and is no link, and neither is a tally that counts the visitor's actions or time in every organ alike (a streak, an activity calendar). A deep link whose parameters one organ computes from the visitor's record is a steering link from that organ to the one it opens. A hyperlink, a deep link with fixed parameters, a shared engine, library, static material or style, and a selection several views share are no link, because the second organ reads nothing the first one wrote.
scope.reach: Reach is the share of the canon's units, as the lab's bindings list them, that the lab's organs work on: an organ works on a unit when it teaches, practises, measures, computes or records something of that unit on the real path, and a unit named only in text, a heading or a placeholder is not worked on. A unit counts toward reach only when enough distinct organs work on it: one at levels 1 and 2, two at level 3, three from level 4 (organs_per_unit). The units are the divisions of an outside source (a syllabus's objectives, a textbook's sections, a catalogue's measured quantities). Where a lab's canon is its own thesis, the rater checks the declared units against the published work the thesis answers to, and reads reach against that work's divisions when the declared units cover only part of it, so a lab cannot widen its reach by narrowing its subject. A lab with no bindings has a reach of 0.
scope.rule: A lab has three levels: its scope level, the highest level whose thresholds its graph meets, counting up from level 1 with no level skipped; and its product level and its subject level, each min(lower median of its axis rungs, weakest axis + 2) and neither above its scope level. The lab's level is the lowest of the three. At levels 1 and 2 every organ and every link counts. From level 3 an organ counts only when it belongs to the largest connected part of the graph, with links read in either direction, only the links inside that part count, and the instrument must belong to it; from level 4 at least one other organ reads what the visitor did on the instrument, and from level 5 at least two. From level 4 the graph holds the stated number of steering links and a directed cycle made of them. At level 5, each product axis the lab marks not applicable, with its reason, lowers the organ floor by the organs that axis carries in Claude Prep's joined graph (organ_of, each organ once) and the link floor by two for each of them, to no fewer than 4 organs and no fewer links than the level's steering links. Above level 5 the steps between levels stay as the thresholds state them, added to that lowered floor. No level below 5 asks such a lab for more organs or links than its level 5 floor, so the lowered floor can be reached, and a level that asks for a link still asks for one. An axis grade is a rung, never a level, and is always shown with the lab's graph beside it, so a deep rung on a one-organ lab never reads as a deep lab.

claude_prep.how_counted: Counted at the anchor commit from the inventory of its 437 features in 28 areas, by the definitions above, on the owner's path: the hosted copy is sealed to a private course repository, so a public visitor reaches only the form that connects a token. Each feature was assigned to the organ whose work it does, or to the shell, data and tooling that carry organs. Nine organs: the Today view (next actions computed from the record); lessons (course, module and lesson pages with checks, notes and guides); drills (every untimed mode with the help panel, the tutored mocks, warm-ups and the spaced review of misses, which run in one runner); the timed mock exam (its deadline, navigator, flags and exam report; every session, drills included, ends on one results screen whose revision sheet of misses is built in the browser, never stored, and belongs to the session it reports); the flashcard deck; the progress view (mastery, readiness, history, calibration); the plan (exam dates, daily minutes, the pace meter, phases); the hands-on labs; and the tracker of the official courses. The instrument is drills: the runner where the visitor answers and the app grades the answer, which is the mechanism the other organs read; Today, progress and lessons each compute from what the visitor did there, and the timed mock exam is the summative challenge beside it. Not organs: shell, search, settings, sync, editions, design system, tests, and the agent commands that run outside the app, off the page's real path. Fourteen links, each an ordered pair where one organ computes from what another wrote: Today reads lessons (the next lesson), flashcards (cards due), drills (misses and the weakest objective) and progress (the focus course is the first one not yet ready); progress reads drills (mastery), the mock (readiness checks) and lessons (lessons done); lessons read drills (checks dealt unseen first, then last wrong); drills read lessons (warm-ups scoped to studied lessons, and completed lessons with no answers join the weak list) and the mock (its misses open a drill); the plan reads lessons (the pace divides the lessons left); and Today opens lessons, drills and flashcards with parameters it computes from the record. Ten of them steer; the four that progress and the plan read only show. The labs and the course tracker appear on other pages only as panels, and no organ computes from their state, so the largest connected part holds seven organs, drills and the mock among them. Every one of the 27 domains and of the 123 objectives has a lesson, at least 3 questions and at least one card, and a mastery state, so four organs work on each unit. Counted the same way at the commits its history dates to levels 2, 3 and 4, the graph already had these nine organs and fourteen links when the app was rebuilt at level 2: its breadth arrived whole and its later levels were depth, so its history bounds thresholds 2 to 4 from above and cannot set them.

graph.reads: Each link runs from the organ that wrote to the organ that reads it. Counted by tools/evolution.mjs, which fails when these counts and the numbers above disagree.

1.says: One organ, or several that do not read each other: the lab is a single working part, however well it is drawn and however many units it touches.

2.says: At least three organs and the first link: one organ computes from what another wrote, as a record view turns the sessions practice finished into a state per unit, over a quarter of the declared units.

3.says: At least five organs in one connected graph, the instrument among them, joined by at least four links, with half the declared units each worked on by two organs; an organ outside the largest connected part counts for nothing.

4.says: At least six joined organs and seven links, three of which steer, with a directed loop made of steering links, so a result made in one organ changes what another offers next; another organ reads what the visitor did on the instrument, and four fifths of the declared units are each worked on by three organs.

5.says: At least seven joined organs and eleven links, five of which steer, with two organs reading what the visitor did on the instrument and three organs working on every declared unit. Claude Prep measures nine organs, seven of them joined by fourteen links, ten of which steer. Each product axis marked not applicable lowers the floor by its organs in organ_of.

6.says: The level 5 graph with the organs that stood apart now reading the visitor's record, and a forecast organ that answers from the model of that visitor with an interval: at least nine joined organs and sixteen links, more than the anchor measurably has.

7.says: A comparison organ joins: it computes the differences between the visitor's record and a shared one unit by unit, reads the record view and the summative challenge, and is read by the record view: at least ten joined organs and nineteen links.

8.says: A workshop organ joins: a contributor drafts an entry and runs the lab's gates on it, and practice and lessons read the draft before it is submitted: at least eleven joined organs and twenty-one links.

9.says: A release organ joins: the visitor opens a released dataset, filters it and places their own result in it from their record, and the instrument opens any released case: at least twelve joined organs and twenty-three links.

10.says: A citation organ joins: the visitor picks any state and gets a citation pinned to a release, beside the verified outside references to that part, read from the release and comparison organs: at least thirteen joined organs and twenty-five links over every unit.

ledger_schema.entry: url, date (when the rater verified it), quote (the context that points to the lab), kind (course, article, forum, paper, documentation), owner (who controls the page), axes (the atlas axes it references)
ledger_schema.independent: Two entries are independent when different people or organisations own their pages. No entry may be owned or controlled by Luis or by the lab's builders.
ledger_schema.rule: Rung 10 on an axis holds when the ledger lists at least 5 independent entries that reference that axis's object and the rater has verified each at its URL.

bindings_schema.rule: Every lab ladder on the atlas declares its bindings before grading. A rater grades no axis whose binding is missing, and records it as ungraded, never as 0. Product rungs that say canon, curriculum, unit, track, challenge, central scene or known setup failure read these fields.

fields.canon: Object: name, source (author and year, or a URL) and kind (course, textbook, catalogue, standard, source fiction, or the lab's thesis).
fields.units: Array of at least 1: id, name, and weight in percent where the canon gives one.
fields.challenge_blueprint: Object: units (unit id to weight in percent, summing to 100), formats (the item formats the challenge uses), items (a count) and minutes; or {"na": "<reason of at least 20 characters>"} where the lab has no summative challenge.
fields.central_scene: Object: description and source (the scene, page or thesis sentence the lab reproduces).
fields.fiction_inventory: Array of at least 10: id, capability, detail (the depicted level of detail) and source (scene, page or thesis sentence).
fields.known_setup_failures: Array of at least 1: id, failure and diagnosis (the plain-language text the page shows); or {"na": "<reason of at least 20 characters>"} where nothing can fail at setup.

optional.curriculum: Object: name, source and the items it maps onto units; material rung 4 needs it.
optional.tracks: Array: id and name, grouping units.
optional.own_material: What 'the visitor's own material' means in this lab.
optional.protagonist_verbs: The actions of the fiction's protagonist (interaction rung 5).
optional.signature_move: The world's signature move bound to state (graphics rung 5).

axes.name: Orientation and next action

Load a seeded record (the lab's demo record or a saved export) and reopen: read the entry view for continue, due, weakest unit and goal countdown, and follow each as a link. Open every deep-link parameter with a valid, an empty and a malformed value. Finish one activity and follow its next actions. Trigger each known setup failure from the bindings and read its diagnosis.
